cues.text: Imagine it's Friday morning. You're at the airport, coffee in hand, ready to fly.
And then every screen in the building turns blue.
The check-in desks. The departure boards. The gates. All of them. Same blue screen.
And it's not just your airport. It's happening in banks, hospitals, supermarkets, TV stations… all over the world. At the same time.
This was July 19th, 2024. And it wasn't a hack.
It was one file. A file smaller than a photo on your phone. With one tiny thing too many inside it.
This is how one extra number crashed eight and a half million computers.
To understand what happened, you need to meet the guard.
Hello. I protect your computer. Very important job.
Big companies don't just use normal antivirus. They use security software like CrowdStrike Falcon, a guard that watches everything happening on the computer, all the time.
And to see everything, the guard doesn't stand at the front door. It lives in the basement.
That basement is called the kernel. It's the deepest part of Windows, where the computer talks directly to its own hardware.
Down there, the guard can stop almost any attack. But there's a catch. In the kernel, there's no such thing as a small mistake.
If a normal app crashes, the app closes. If something in the kernel crashes, Windows has no safe way to keep going.
So it does the only safe thing it can. It stops everything. And shows you a blue screen.
Now, hackers invent new tricks every day. So the guard needs new instructions every day too.
CrowdStrike sends those instructions in small update files, straight to millions of computers. No restart. No button to click. They just arrive.
Think of it like a delivery. Every package comes with a form, and the guard knows exactly how many boxes are on that form.
For one type of form, the guard expected twenty boxes.
At 4:09 in the morning, UTC, a new update went out. And that form had twenty-one.
Seventeen. Eighteen. Nineteen. Twenty…
Twenty… one?
When the guard reached for box number twenty-one, it reached into memory that didn't belong to it. And in the kernel, that's fatal.
Crash.
But here's the cruel part. When the computer restarted, the guard woke up first, read the same file again…
…and crashed again. And again. And again.
Within minutes, the blue screens spread across the planet.
Flights were grounded. Hospitals went back to pen and paper. Payment machines stopped. Some TV channels went off the air.
Microsoft later estimated that eight and a half million Windows computers went down.
And here's the crazy part: that was less than one percent of all Windows machines.
Less than one percent. But it was the one percent that runs airports, banks and hospitals.
If this kind of story is your thing, hit subscribe. It's free, and unlike this update, it won't crash anything.
CrowdStrike spotted the problem fast. About an hour and twenty minutes after the update went out, they pulled it.
Problem solved, right?
Not even close. Because a computer stuck in a crash loop can't download a fix.
So the fix had to be done by hand. Someone had to walk up to each broken computer, start it in safe mode, find one file, and delete it.
One computer at a time. Now imagine you're the IT person, and your company has fifty thousand of them.
And many of those machines were encrypted with BitLocker. So before you could even delete the file, you needed a long recovery key. For every single machine.
Some companies reportedly kept those keys on servers… that had also crashed.
It took days. CrowdStrike said that by July 29th, ten days later, about ninety-nine percent of its Windows sensors were back online.
So how much did one extra number cost?

Delta Air Lines says it had to cancel about seven thousand flights, affecting more than a million passengers. It sued CrowdStrike for over five hundred million dollars. CrowdStrike says Delta's own slow recovery was the real problem.
An insurance firm called Parametrix estimated that the biggest US companies alone lost about five point four billion dollars.
And to say sorry to the partners who helped clean up, CrowdStrike sent them a ten dollar Uber Eats gift card.
Which some people couldn't use… because Uber flagged it as fraud.
Ten dollars. For a five billion dollar Friday.
So how did a mistake this simple get past a company this big?
According to CrowdStrike's own report, the tool that was supposed to check these files had a bug of its own. It let the bad file through.
And the update went to everyone at once. No small test group first. No slow rollout.
Since then, CrowdStrike says it now checks the number of fields, sends updates in rings, a small group first, then everyone, and lets customers choose when they get them.
The lesson is bigger than one company. The more of the world runs on the same software, the smaller the mistake it takes to stop it.
So here's my question. Who's really to blame? The company that shipped the file… or a world that let one update reach millions of computers at once? Tell me in the comments.
And subscribe, because next time, people found a way to steal Instagram accounts… by politely asking an AI.
Twenty boxes. Always twenty. I check now.
